description: What is grown, as a record rather than as a string typed into each block. A Crop carries the four facts every other feature keeps asking for and nobody had anywhere to put: how long it takes to make fruit, when that fruit comes off, how many days must pass between the last spray and the first pick, and which varieties are actually planted. THIS IS A MASTER, NOT A PLANTING. It says what a Sweet Cherry is, not which block has one — Field.crop names the crop growing on a block and stays free text, because a block of table grapes is not a schema change and never was. THE PHI IS THE REASON THIS DOCTYPE EXISTS RATHER THAN A SELECT. A pre-harvest interval is a legal number: spray on Tuesday with a 7-day PHI and fruit picked on Sunday cannot be sold. That number belongs to the crop-and-chemical pair, and until something on the site knew what a crop WAS, the crop half of it had nowhere to live and every check had to take it on trust from the caller.

fields.description: What the crop is called in the words a grower uses — 'Sweet Cherry', 'Apple', 'Pear'. IT IS THE DOCNAME, so it is the string every other record spells when it names a crop, and it is why this doctype does not allow rename: a crop that can be re-keyed is a crop whose name on last season's records means something else this season.
fields.label: Crop Name

fields.description: The binomial — 'Prunus avium' for sweet cherry, 'Malus domestica' for apple. Optional, and worth having: a pesticide label, an ODA registration and an export phytosanitary certificate are all written in Latin, and matching them to 'cherry' is a judgement somebody makes twice a season.
fields.label: Scientific Name

fields.description: The commercial grouping the crop is handled and sold in. IT IS A HANDLING CATEGORY, NOT A TAXONOMY — 'Tree Fruit' here means the pome fruit a packing house runs on one line, and 'Stone Fruit' the drupes it runs on another, which is the distinction a packout sheet and a price list actually draw. Where the two ways of grouping disagree, this column follows the packing house, because that is who the number is for. 'Other' is real and is not a placeholder: a cover crop and a nursery block belong to a farm's records without belonging to any of the four.
fields.label: Crop Type
fields.options:
Tree Fruit
Stone Fruit
Berry
Vegetable
Other

fields.description: Whether the planting lives across seasons. THIS IS WHAT MAKES `maturity_years` MEANINGFUL OR A CONTRADICTION: a perennial has years of non-bearing growth to capitalise before it earns anything, and an annual has none — so a variety row claiming three years to maturity on an Annual crop is refused rather than stored. Defaulted to Perennial because this app was built for tree fruit and that is the honest default, not a neutral one.
fields.label: Growth Cycle

fields.description: Whether this crop is grown under a certified organic programme on this operation. A FACT ABOUT THE FARM'S PROGRAMME, NOT ABOUT THE SPECIES — apples are not organic, an apple block under an NOP certificate is. It sits here because a crop is where the spray rules are read from and the organic answer changes which materials are even eligible; a farm running conventional and organic blocks of one crop should leave this off and let the block-level record carry it.
fields.label: Organic Certified

fields.description: The share of this crop's volume sold direct — farm stand, farmers' market, u-pick, direct-to-retail — as a TYPED NUMBER somebody asserts, not a computed one. It is the fallback, and it is labelled as one on purpose: the true figure is direct revenue over total revenue read off Sales Invoice with each customer's sales_channel, and where the invoice data supports that, the computed figure wins and this is shown beside it as a disagreement. It exists because the survey is due in February whether or not that year's invoices are clean, and a number labelled as asserted beats a blank. Leave it empty rather than typing 0 for a crop nobody has estimated: nothing sold direct and nobody asked are different answers.
fields.label: Direct-Marketed %

fields.description: Days from the start of the season to picking. FOR A PERENNIAL THIS IS DAYS FROM BLOOM, and for an annual it is days from planting — the two are different questions and this one column answers whichever the growth cycle implies, because a farm that grows both does not want two columns of which one is always empty. Left blank when nobody has measured it; zero would claim same-day harvest.
fields.label: Days to Harvest

fields.description: The month picking normally starts. A WINDOW IS STATED AS BOTH ENDS OR NEITHER: a start with no end is a season nothing closes, and the controller refuses it rather than storing half a window that every reader has to guess the other half of. The window is allowed to wrap the year end — a start of November and an end of February is a real harvest, and refusing it would be refusing the southern hemisphere and the greenhouse both.
fields.label: Harvest Window Start
fields.options:
January
February
March
April
May
June
July
August
September
October
November
December

fields.description: The month picking normally finishes. See `harvest_window_start` — both ends or neither, and wrapping the year end is allowed.
fields.label: Harvest Window End
fields.options:
January
February
March
April
May
June
July
August
September
October
November
December

fields.description:
The soluble-solids figure a block of this crop is picked at, in degrees Brix. THE NUMBER THE HARVEST-READINESS OVERLAY ARGUES A PICK DATE FROM, read beside the BBCH code off the latest Crop Observation — the doctype's own note says why neither number alone will call a pick right: Brix rises while the stage stands still in a hot week, and the stage advances while Brix stalls in a wet one.

A CROP-LEVEL FLOOR AND NOT A CONTRACT SPECIFICATION. It is the figure that colours a map, and a buyer's minimum is a term of a sale that lives on the sale. A variety may depart from it — `Crop Variety.target_brix` is the sparse overlay, resolved per variety, with the answer reporting which of the two it used. Left blank the overlay reports the stage alone and NAMES the missing target rather than assuming one; a fabricated Brix target would turn every block on the farm the same colour on the same day.
fields.label: Target Brix

fields.description: The pre-harvest interval in days: the minimum that must pass between the last application and the first pick. A FLOOR, NOT THE ANSWER. The binding PHI is the one on the label of the material actually applied, and it varies by chemical on one crop from zero days to thirty; this column is the crop's own default for the case where nothing more specific is known, and a check that finds a label PHI must prefer it. Stored here rather than inferred because zero and 'nobody recorded one' are different facts and a spray gate has to be able to tell them apart — 0 means genuinely no interval, blank means unknown. See `list_crops`, which reports the crops still carrying no PHI.
fields.label: Default PHI (days)

fields.description: The varieties of this crop that are actually planted or actually traded. A CHILD TABLE RATHER THAN A DOCTYPE because a variety has no life apart from its crop: 'Bing' means nothing without 'Sweet Cherry' in front of it, nothing links to a variety on its own, and a top-level doctype would buy a docname nobody needs and a second register to keep in step. Two rows may not share a variety name — a duplicate is two rows about one tree, and every read that groups by variety would double it.
fields.label: Varieties

fields.description: What the crop needs at each stage of its year. THE STAGE IS THE UNIT, NOT THE MONTH, because bloom moves a fortnight between a warm spring and a cold one and a schedule pinned to April waters the wrong week in both. An irrigation plan reads the stage it is currently in and gets a rate; the calendar that maps stage to date belongs to the season, not to the species. Optional in full — a crop with no rows here simply has no modelled demand, which is honest, and is different from a crop modelled as needing nothing.
fields.label: Water Requirements by Growth Stage
Variety Overrides and Protocols
fields.description: Where one variety departs from the crop. BOTH TABLES ARE SPARSE BY DESIGN: a row exists only where a variety genuinely differs, and everything not named here falls back to the crop's own figures above. A form that asked for every stage of every variety would be asking a farm to restate numbers that were already right, and the restatements are what drift.

fields.label: Variety Water Overrides
fields.description: Per-variety departures from the water demand above, by stage. READ AS AN OVERLAY, NEVER AS A REPLACEMENT — a resolver asks this table for (variety, stage), and falls back to the crop's row for that stage when there is none, so a variety with two rows here still has all seven stages answered. Two rows may not name the same variety and stage: which one an irrigation plan read would depend on row order.

fields.label: Variety Cultural Practice Protocols
fields.description: How each variety is grown rather than what it is: GA timings, the PGR program, the thinning approach, the pruning it wants. ONE ROW IS ONE STEP, so a program with three applications is three rows and keeps its schedule where something can read it. This is the farm's intention for a normal year; what was actually applied to a block is a Spray Application, and nothing here is a label.

name: Crop
